_about: Which regions of each repository addon someone must edit before that addon is safe to ship.
Read by the repo-builder skill at generation time; see apps/repo-builder/src/references/generate.md step 2 and references/addon-adoption.md.
A sibling of repository-addons/ rather than a file inside it, because anything inside that directory looks like an addon to copy.

Never copied into a generated repository. In-file guidance inside the addons themselves is deliberately NOT deduplicated against this file: that guidance serves the person adopting the file by hand in a repository that has no manifest.
Occasion lives in docs/github_repository_structure.md and pairing lives in the skill's references/addon-adoption.md. Neither is repeated here.
slots replace a token with a value. reviews demand a judgement with no token to grep for. external happens outside the repository entirely.
value_key groups one answer asked once: the repository owner is spelled three ways across three files.

reviews.section: the variables listed, against what the code actually reads
reviews.decision: The shipped entries are shapes -- an endpoint, an empty credential, a local override -- and none of them is a variable this repository has. Replace them with the real ones and delete the rest. The two ways it goes wrong are silent in opposite directions: a variable the code requires and this file omits fails at run time in someone else's checkout, with an error naming a key rather than the file it belongs in; a variable listed here that nothing reads sends them looking for a value to supply that is never consumed.

reviews.section: every value written into it
reviews.decision: This file is committed and .env is not, which is the point of the pair and also its hazard: everything here is published. Give each variable its shape and never a working value. gitleaks runs at pre-commit and catches the formats it knows -- an AWS key, a GitHub token, a private key block -- and does not know a password, a database URL with credentials in it, or a token this project invented, so one of those reaches the remote with every check green. A real value committed once stays in the history after the next commit deletes it.

external.step: Confirm the destination ignores .env and does not ignore this file: `git check-ignore -v .env .env.example` should name a rule for the first and nothing for the second.
external.consequence: The file's own first paragraph tells the reader that .env is gitignored and this one is not. That is true of the payload's .gitignore, and the addon is adopted into repositories whose .gitignore has been edited since. If the negation is missing, this file is ignored and the clone it exists to serve never sees it; if the .env rule is missing, the file's assurance is false at the moment someone fills a real credential into the copy beside it.

slots.what: The project name, in the H1 header and again in the About and Features text. Shared with CONTRIBUTING.md and CITATION.cff, so it is the same answer asked once. A visible bracket rather than a silent REPLACE- token because a README renders to humans and nothing validates it: an unfilled copy shows a giant placeholder heading, which is the loud failure this scaffold wants. If the logo already carries the name, the H1 is redundant -- the images review covers dropping one.

The one-line description under the title and reused in the About opener -- what the project is, in a breath. A new answer not shared with any other addon: CONTRIBUTING and CITATION carry a name but no tagline. Visible bracket for the same reason as the title, and it renders in the most-read line of the file after the name.

The repository owner in the badge image URLs, the clone URL, and the acknowledgements line. Shared with the repo-owner answer other addons ask for. An empty value gives shields.io badges that render broken and a clone command that fails -- loud, which is the point. Note the space in the token: it makes the URL malformed until replaced, so a half-finished badge cannot pass for a working one.

The repository name in the same badge URLs, the clone URL and directory, and the Homebrew example. Shared with the repo-name answer other addons ask for. Same loud-failure rationale as the owner token.

reviews.section: the logo and hero images in the centered header
reviews.decision: The header references docs/assets/logo.svg and docs/assets/hero.png as relative paths. GitHub renders those from the repository, so until the files exist they show as broken-image icons -- a loud failure by design, paired with the external step that adds them. Either supply the images or delete the blocks and lead with the heading alone. A logo that already spells the project name makes the H1 redundant; keep one, not both. This is a review rather than a slot because the decision is keep-or-cut plus a file to author, not a token to fill.

reviews.section: the badge row under the title
reviews.decision: The scaffold ships three shields.io badges (build, license, release). Keep only the ones backed by something real. A build badge for a workflow that does not exist, or a hardcoded version that is not the current release, renders green-and-official while being false -- the single failure mode a README must not have, because a badge reads as machine-verified fact. Delete any badge you cannot back. Once the owner/repo slots are filled the URLs resolve; an unfilled or unbacked badge renders broken or wrong, which is the loud signal to fix or cut it.

reviews.section: the About, Features, and Usage body content
reviews.decision: Every line of prose, every feature bullet, the comparison table, and the usage example ship as placeholder text, not truth. Replace them with the project's real description, features, and a runnable example. The scaffold's job is the shape and the Markdown palette; the content is entirely the operator's. Trim the Features subsections and the comparison table to what is real, or delete them.

reviews.section: the Install and Usage command blocks
reviews.decision: The fenced commands (brew install, git clone, build-from-source, --help) are stack-specific and, like CONTRIBUTING.md's setup section, do not exist until this repository's first language manifest does -- until then there is nothing real to run. Replace them with the project's actual install and run steps when they exist; until then say so in a line rather than shipping a command that fails. A review, not a slot, because there is no single token: the whole block is either made true or replaced.

reviews.section: the Contributing, Security, and License links
reviews.decision: The scaffold links CONTRIBUTING.md, CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md, SECURITY.md, and LICENSE -- each a separate addon. Keep a link only if that file was actually adopted; otherwise rewrite the line to point at the channel that is real, or delete the section. A README that links a governance or security file the repository does not have is the same dead-link failure CONTRIBUTING.md's conditional links guard against. ADOPT comments mark each.

reviews.section: the table of contents
reviews.decision: The TOC links to headings by their GitHub auto-anchor (lowercase, spaces to hyphens). It must track the headings actually kept -- renaming or deleting a section without fixing the list leaves a dead anchor that scrolls nowhere. No token marks this because the anchors are valid as shipped; it becomes a defect only when the headings change and the list does not.

external.step: Add the images the header references -- docs/assets/logo.svg and docs/assets/hero.png (any format is fine; match the src attributes) -- or delete the header and hero blocks that point at them.
external.consequence: GitHub renders relative image paths from the repository, so until the files are committed the README opens with broken-image icons where the logo and hero should be. Nothing else reports them missing -- the render is the only check, which is why this is loud on purpose rather than a silent gap. Add real assets or remove the references so the file does not ship pointing at images that are not there.

slots.token: [REPLACE: the private security address you monitor]
slots.what: The private channel a vulnerability report is sent to, in the Reporting a vulnerability section. A visible bracket rather than a silent REPLACE- token, on purpose and for the same reason the Code of Conduct's reporting line is: this is the one field whose failure mode is being trusted, so an unfilled copy has to announce itself in the rendered policy rather than quietly route reports into a void. Kept as a separate answer from conduct-contact even though a solo maintainer may use one address for both, because the security channel is often a different inbox or team. If the operator chooses GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting instead of email (the review below), this token is deleted rather than filled -- the reviews and external step cover that path.

reviews.section: the reporting channel in Reporting a vulnerability -- email versus GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting
reviews.decision: The file ships with an email address as the channel and PVR as the documented alternative; the repository has to name exactly one. PVR is GitHub's recommended private channel -- a Report a vulnerability button on the Security tab that needs no shared inbox -- but it is a repository setting that must be enabled first (the external step below) and is offered on public repositories, or private ones with GitHub Advanced Security, not on a private repository on the free plan. Choose email or PVR, fill or delete the slot accordingly, rewrite the paragraph to describe the one channel that is real, and delete the other. A file that names both, or names PVR without enabling it, points reporters at a route that does not answer.

reviews.section: the acknowledgement window in What to expect
reviews.decision: The section promises an acknowledgement within a stated window and coordinated disclosure. A window is a commitment a reporter measures the project against, so state a number only if it will be kept -- a promised three days that becomes three weeks is the same broken trust this file exists to prevent, surfacing at the worst moment. Where no window can be committed to, say so in words rather than inventing one. No token marks this because the shipped wording is already honest as a default; it becomes a defect only when someone writes a number they cannot hold.

reviews.section: the Supported versions table
reviews.decision: The shipped table (1.x supported, < 1.0 not) is a plausible-looking guess that validates and renders while telling users which versions are maintained -- a silent failure when it is wrong, not an error any tool catches. Replace its rows with the versions this project actually supports, or, for a project with a single release line or one still before its first release, delete the table and state the policy in a sentence. This is a review rather than a slot because there is no single token to fill: the whole table is either made true or removed.

external.step: If GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting is the chosen channel, enable it at Settings -> Advanced Security -> Private vulnerability reporting.
external.consequence: Without it the Report a vulnerability button never appears, so a policy pointing reporters at the Security tab routes them to a form that does not exist. Nothing in this repository reports whether it is on -- unlike CODEOWNERS, no script checks this -- and it is offered on public repositories or private ones with GitHub Advanced Security, not on a private repository on the free plan, the same plan boundary scripts/repo-settings check reports for push protection and rulesets. Skip this step entirely if the channel is email.

slots.token: [REPLACE: the support channel you actually read]
slots.what: Where a question goes, in the Where to ask section. A visible bracket rather than a silent REPLACE- token, for the same reason SECURITY.md's reporting address is one: an unfilled copy has to announce itself in the rendered document rather than sending someone to a channel that does not exist. Kept separate from security-contact and conduct-contact -- a question is public and a vulnerability report is not, so the two rarely share a destination even for a solo maintainer.

reviews.section: the channels named in Where to ask
reviews.decision: The file assumes there is somewhere other than the issue tracker to ask, and for many projects there is not. Name the channels that exist -- Discussions, a chat server, a mailing list -- and delete the rest; for a project small enough that one tracker is honest, say so plainly and let the issue forms carry questions too. Whichever destination is named, uncomment the contact_links block the payload already ships commented out in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/config.yml and point it there: that surfaces the destination on the template chooser, one step before the new-issue banner GitHub uses to link this file, which is where someone with a question rather than a bug is still deciding what to open. Both must name the same channel -- two answers to "where do I ask?" reach the same person seconds apart.

reviews.section: the What to expect section
reviews.decision: The shipped wording commits to nothing specific and says the project is maintained on a best-effort basis, which is honest as a default and needs no change to be true. It becomes a defect only when someone replaces it with a response time the project cannot hold -- a stated window that slips is worse than no statement, because a person waits on it instead of looking elsewhere. No token marks this for that reason.

reviews.section: what this file does not route
reviews.decision: A vulnerability report is not a support question, and every channel this file names is public. If SECURITY.md was adopted, say so here and send reporters there; if it was not, this file is the only page a reporter reads, so it has to carry a private address of its own. A vulnerability routed into Discussions is disclosed by the act of reporting it.

external.step: If the contact_links block in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/config.yml is uncommented, replace OWNER/REPO in its url before committing.
external.consequence: A contact link renders as a working link. Left as shipped it points at github.com/OWNER/REPO/discussions, a real page belonging to someone else. Nothing here catches it: that file is payload rather than an addon, so it has no entry in this manifest and no adoption walkthrough passes over it.

external.step: If GitHub Discussions is the named channel, enable it at Settings -> General -> Features -> Discussions.
external.consequence: Without it the link points at a tab that is not there. Nothing in this repository reports whether it is on. Skip this step if the channel is a chat server, a mailing list, or the issue tracker itself.

reviews.section: the file name
reviews.decision: GitHub matches the file name to a discussion category slug, so this file serves the General category and nothing else. Rename it to the slug of the category it is for, taking that slug from the category's URL rather than guessing at how a name with an ampersand or a space is spelled. A name matching no category means the form is silently never shown, which is indistinguishable from having no form.

reviews.section: the scope the intro sets
reviews.decision: The form deliberately narrows General to the question documentation could not have anticipated, and sends anything the documentation should have answered to the issue tracker as a defect. That is a routing decision about this project, not a neutral default: a project that would rather answer usage questions in a thread has to edit the intro, because as written it tells those people to leave. Keep the questions and the required flags honest with whatever it says -- a required field someone cannot answer is a reason to close the tab rather than post.

external.step: Enable Discussions at Settings -> General -> Features -> Discussions, and confirm the category this file is named for exists.
external.consequence: Without the feature there is no category to match and the form is inert. Nothing in this repository reports whether it is on.

reviews.section: the file name
reviews.decision: Ideas is one of GitHub's default categories and its slug is `ideas`, so this file usually needs no rename. Confirm it against the category's URL anyway: a category that was renamed, deleted, or recreated has a different slug, and a name matching no category means the form is silently never shown.

reviews.section: the boundary against the issue tracker
reviews.decision: This form asks whether something should be built; the payload's .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/feature_request.yml asks for something to be built. Adopting both without saying which comes first leaves a contributor choosing at random between two forms that look equally correct. Say in CONTRIBUTING.md that an idea is discussed here and filed there, or drop one of the two.

reviews.section: the participation dropdown
reviews.decision: It asks whether the proposer wants to implement the idea, which is only worth asking of a project that accepts outside code. Remove it from a repository that does not, where the honest answer is never the first option and asking implies otherwise.

external.step: Enable Discussions at Settings -> General -> Features -> Discussions, and confirm the Ideas category exists.
external.consequence: Without the feature there is no category to match and the form is inert. Nothing in this repository reports whether it is on.

slots.token: [REPLACE: the maintainer with final authority, as a GitHub @handle]
slots.what: The single person who holds final say, named in the opening section. A visible bracket rather than a silent REPLACE- token because nothing validates GOVERNANCE.md the way GitHub validates CODEOWNERS -- an unfilled handle renders in the published document and no tool reports it, so a human is the only check. Kept as its own answer rather than reused from code-owner or repo-owner: repo-owner may be an organization, which does not make decisions, and code-owner may be a team, which is not a single authority. This is the human who decides -- on a personal repository usually the same handle as both, on an organization repository a person inside it.

reviews.section: the Code of Conduct link in Conduct and disputes
reviews.decision: The line assumes CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md was adopted alongside this file. Keep it only if that addon was taken; delete the paragraph otherwise, so governance does not route a conduct report to a document that is not there. An ADOPT comment marks it.

reviews.section: the single-authority model itself, marked in Changing this document
reviews.decision: The template states a benevolent-dictator model: one maintainer with final say. Confirm that actually describes this project before shipping it. If decisions are already shared among several accountable people, this template is the wrong shape -- it states an authority one of them does not hold alone -- so replace it with a multi-maintainer model rather than filling it in. CNCF publishes templates for the common ones: a self-selecting maintainer council, an elected steering committee, an umbrella of subprojects. This is a review rather than a slot because the whole document is either the right shape or replaced, with no single token to fill.

slots.what: The default owner on the `*` line: @username or @org/team-name, keeping the @. A separate question from repo-owner rather than the same one twice -- on a personal repository they are the same handle, but the owner of an organization repository is the organization, and an organization is not a valid code owner. It has to be a user or a team inside it. The named owner needs write access, and a team must also be visible and hold write access in its own right; an owner who lacks it is silently never assigned. This is the one placeholder in these addons that reports itself, because GitHub validates CODEOWNERS: an unfilled line is highlighted on the file's page and returned by `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/codeowners/errors`.

reviews.section: the per-path block below the `*` line, and the /.github/ and /CODEOWNERS lines under it, all commented out
reviews.decision: Ownership per path is read off the repository's layout, not filled in from a token, which is why it ships commented. Leave it that way while one owner owns everything: a path rule naming the same person as the catch-all adds nothing and has to be kept true as the tree moves. When it is uncommented, every rule must sit BELOW the catch-all, because the last matching pattern wins rather than the most specific, and a path rule above `*` is silently overridden. The two self-ownership lines are GitHub's own recommendation once a second account has write access -- without them anyone can edit this file, or the workflows beside it, in the same pull request that depends on the edit.

reviews.section: the solo-maintainer paragraph at the end
reviews.decision: GitHub does not let the author of a pull request approve it, so `* @you` plus a rule requiring code-owner review makes every pull request you open need an approval only you can give and are not allowed to give. Decide whether to enable that requirement now or keep the file as a record of ownership until a second maintainer exists, then delete the paragraph. Leaving it in ships instructions to readers as part of the file.

external.step: Enable "Require review from Code Owners" on the default branch, through a ruleset or a branch protection rule.
external.consequence: Without it this file only requests a reviewer and nothing waits for the answer: a pull request touching an owned path merges with no code-owner approval and no record that one was expected. `scripts/repo-settings check` reports whether anything actually imposes it, and says so rather than guessing when the answer needs admin to read; rulesets are unavailable on a private repository on the free plan.

external.step: Run `scripts/repo-settings check` once the file is pushed, or `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/codeowners/errors` directly in a repository that does not have that script.
external.consequence: The verification this file gets, and it has to be asked for: an invalid line is skipped and an owner without write access is dropped without either announcing itself in the course of a pull request, so a file that is half in force reads exactly like one that is working. The script calls that endpoint and reports the requirement above in the same run.

slots.what: The project name in the opening heading and welcome line. Shared with CITATION.cff, so it is the same answer asked once. It renders visibly, so an unfilled copy ships a contributing guide that welcomes people to REPLACE-PROJECT-TITLE -- the placeholder announces itself rather than promising something absent, which is why it is a slot and not a review.

reviews.section: the opening paragraph and the one-line project description in it
reviews.decision: The template says how work reaches the branch, which it can, but not what the project is or who it is for, which it cannot. Rewrite the first sentence so it introduces this project rather than a generic one -- an ADOPT comment marks the spot. The rest of the intro is accurate as shipped and needs no change.

reviews.section: the Code of Conduct link in the intro
reviews.decision: The line assumes CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md was taken alongside this file. Keep it only if that addon was adopted; delete the line otherwise, so the guide does not link a file that is not there. An ADOPT comment marks it.

reviews.section: the security carve-out under Reporting a bug
reviews.decision: It links SECURITY.md and tells contributors to report vulnerabilities there instead of in a public issue. Keep the link only if that addon was adopted; otherwise replace it with the private channel you actually watch, or delete the paragraph. A guide that routes a vulnerability report to a channel that does not exist is the same silent failure the Code of Conduct's reporting line guards against -- worse than saying nothing, because someone relies on it at the worst moment.

reviews.section: the Ways to contribute list
reviews.decision: Trim it to the paths this project can actually shepherd. Advertising a contribution type no maintainer has time to mentor invites work that then stalls, which reads worse than not inviting it. An ADOPT comment marks the list.

reviews.section: Setting up your environment
reviews.decision: The section documents the scripts/ wrappers, which ship correct and stay correct. The concrete build and test commands are stack-specific and do not exist until the repository's first language manifest does -- until then scripts/check reports nothing to run, and that is honest. Fill in the stack-specific steps when a manifest lands; leave the section pointing at the wrappers until then. The wrappers are not a placeholder to replace, so this is a review rather than a slot.

reviews.section: how anyone reaches it
reviews.decision: Nothing in GitHub's interface offers a named template. A pull request gets .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md unless the URL asks for this file by name with ?expand=1&template=<name>.md, which means hand-editing a URL. The payload's .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md ships the fix commented out at the top -- a line of links that become clickable from that description's Preview tab. Uncomment it, and keep only the templates actually adopted. Left commented, this is a template nobody opens, and nothing reports that.

reviews.section: whether this repository releases this way
reviews.decision: The questions assume a tagged version cut from a range of commits, with a changelog entry to match. A project that publishes continuously, or from a branch rather than a tag, is answering a form about a process it does not run -- and a form answered mechanically stops being read. Rewrite it around the release this project actually performs, or do not adopt it.

reviews.section: the checklist
reviews.decision: Its first and third items reference a changelog; the second, on the version being recorded consistently, does not and stays either way. Adopted without the CHANGELOG.md addon, the changelog items ask a reviewer to check a file that is not there, and the usual outcome is a ticked box meaning nothing. Drop those two or adopt the changelog.

reviews.section: how anyone reaches it
reviews.decision: Nothing in GitHub's interface offers a named template. A pull request gets .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md unless the URL asks for this file by name with ?expand=1&template=<name>.md, which means hand-editing a URL. The payload's .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md ships the fix commented out at the top -- a line of links that become clickable from that description's Preview tab. Uncomment it, and keep only the templates actually adopted. Left commented, this is a template nobody opens, and nothing reports that.

reviews.section: what counts as a hotfix here
reviews.decision: This template is shorter than the default, which makes it the path of least resistance for anyone in a hurry. It stays rare only if the bar is written down: production impact, and a cost to waiting that is stated rather than assumed. Put that bar in CONTRIBUTING.md next to adopting this file, or the exception becomes the fast lane.

reviews.section: the last checklist item
reviews.decision: It asks whether the fix landed on every branch that needs it, which presumes a release line separate from the default branch. On a repository with one long-lived branch there is nothing to answer and the item trains people to tick without reading. Remove it unless the project really maintains more than one.

slots.token: [NOTE: describe your means of reporting here.]
slots.what: The reporting channel for a violation. Unlike a silent REPLACE- token this renders visibly in the published document, so an unadopted Code of Conduct announces itself rather than quietly promising a channel that does not exist. That is the one thing worse than having no Code of Conduct, and it is why the visible marker is kept rather than normalized.

reviews.section: Addressing and Repairing Harm
reviews.decision: Upstream ships suggested remedies and marks them for replacement. Confirm they describe how this project actually responds, or rewrite them. Remedies nobody intends to apply are worse than none, because the document is what a reporter is told to rely on.

reviews.section: Appendix: How to Apply These Terms to Your New Programs
reviews.decision: The angle-bracket fields there are GPL instructional text describing what to put in YOUR source files and --version output. Do not edit them in LICENSE; the file ships verbatim and is not ours to re-mark.

reviews.section: or-later versus only
reviews.decision: LICENSE cannot express the choice -- its text is identical either way. Record it in the per-file SPDX headers and in CITATION.cff if that addon is also taken. Relicensing to a future GPLv4 needs every contributor's consent once the project has history, which is why the payload's own docs choose or-later.

slots.what: The project name, as it will read inside the copyright notices in the source files: "The <project> Authors". Shared with README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, CITATION.cff, _config.yml, and .devcontainer/devcontainer.json, so it is the same answer asked once.

The first copyright holder, as a legal name rather than a GitHub handle -- the person or the company that owns the copyright, since those are frequently not the same and only one of them is enforceable.

reviews.section: the source files this file exists to serve
reviews.decision: Adopting AUTHORS is half a change. Its value is that copyright notices in the source tree stop naming individuals and read "Copyright (C) <year> The <project> Authors" instead, with an SPDX line above them, so the list changes in one place. Write those notices in the same change. Without them this is a list nothing references, and it will be out of date before anyone notices it is not being read.

reviews.section: whether the project needs it
reviews.decision: It earns its place when contributions arrive from more than one legal entity, when a contributor agreement is in play, or when files are likely to be copied out of this repository on their own. A single-author project gets nothing from it that a name in the notice does not already give, and gains a second list to keep current.

reviews.section: LICENSE is not edited to match
reviews.decision: It cannot be. LICENSE is the license text reproduced verbatim under its own terms, and the angle-bracket fields in its appendix are instructions describing what to write in your source files -- not blanks to fill in there. Every change this addon implies happens in the source tree, in README.md, and in CITATION.cff if that addon is also taken.

reviews.section: who keeps it current
reviews.decision: Nothing generates this file and no check notices when a new entity starts contributing without being added. Name the moment it gets updated -- reviewing a first pull request from a new employer, or countersigning an agreement -- in CONTRIBUTING.md. A copyright list maintained by whoever remembers is a copyright list that is wrong.

slots.what: Repository owner in the Unreleased compare link at the bottom.
Repository name in the same link.

reviews.section: The <Replace ...> note between the intro and [Unreleased]
reviews.decision: Instructions, not content. Delete the whole block once the link is filled, or it ships to readers as part of the changelog.

reviews.section: the categories, against this repository's label vocabulary
reviews.decision: The shipped categories key on `*` and on `dependencies`, the label Dependabot applies to its own pull requests, so the file is true of a repository on its first day. Extend it only with labels that exist and are actually applied -- a category naming an unused label renders as no heading at all, which reads as "no changes of that kind" rather than as a typo. For a repository set up by /setup-matt-pocock-skills, docs/agents/ records the triage label vocabulary this should agree with.

reviews.section: which paths actually reach this file
reviews.decision: It is read whenever GitHub generates release notes: the Generate release notes button, the POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/releases/generate-notes endpoint, and scripts/release, which passes --generate-notes only for a repository with no CHANGELOG.md. So a repository publishing from its changelog still reaches this file, just never through scripts/release -- do not read a green release as evidence the categories are right when the first thing to exercise them will be someone clicking the button.

external.step: Install the All Contributors app on the repository from https://github.com/apps/allcontributors
external.consequence: Without it the @allcontributors comment syntax does nothing and nothing reports that -- the comment simply sits there and no pull request appears.

slots.what: projectOwner. Required, and the CLI throws rather than guessing, so this failure is at least loud. It builds the profile and commit links, so a wrong value gives a table of dead links instead of an error.
projectName. Same.
title. Every active REPLACE- value here is schema-valid, so a half-filled file validates, renders, and hands out a BibTeX entry crediting the placeholder. Nothing warns anyone.
authors[0].family-names.
authors[0].given-names.
repository-code URL.
repository-code URL.

reviews.section: the commented-out license: line
reviews.decision: The one field where a placeholder cannot pass -- license is a closed SPDX enum, so a placeholder fails validation and the sidebar renders an error instead of a citation. It ships commented rather than wrong. Uncomment and fill it, or the citation carries no license.

reviews.section: the commented version / date-released / doi block
reviews.decision: Left commented because a template cannot keep them true and a stale value cites a version that was never released. Fill them when something releases, and again when something releases again.

reviews.section: preferred-citation
reviews.decision: It REPLACES the citation rather than supplementing it -- the sidebar stops citing the software and starts citing the article. Uncomment only if that is genuinely what you want.

reviews.section: every platform entry
reviews.decision: All ship commented out, which is the correct state until an account exists. Uncomment only lines whose account is real and replace USERNAME. Nothing validates these: an uncommented placeholder is not an error, it is a working button pointing at a stranger's donation page.

slots.what: The site title, rendered in the theme's header and in the browser tab. Shared with CITATION.cff and CONTRIBUTING.md, so it is the same answer asked once.
The site description, rendered by most themes under the title and used in the feed metadata. One sentence saying what the project is.

reviews.section: whether Pages builds with Jekyll at all
reviews.decision: This file is read when the Pages source is "Deploy from a branch". A site published by a GitHub Actions workflow is built however that workflow says, and this file is inert there unless the workflow runs Jekyll itself -- adopted into that setup it is a config nothing reads, which looks like configuration and is not.

reviews.section: the exclude list
reviews.decision: Jekyll copies anything it does not recognize into the published site, so every path that is the project rather than the site has to be named. Two things about the shipped list. It repeats Jekyll's own default exclusions on purpose -- GitHub Pages pins Jekyll 3, where the `exclude` key replaces the defaults instead of adding to them, so dropping those lines is how a repository starts publishing node_modules/. And the entries after them are this repository's own directories, which is only right while the site lives outside all of them: delete the line for whichever directory holds the site, and add whatever this repository added beside them. What is missed is published, not flagged.

reviews.section: the theme
reviews.decision: minima is the default GitHub Pages theme and renders. Change it to any other supported theme, or to a remote_theme, before deciding the site looks the way it should.

external.step: Turn on Pages at Settings -> Pages and set the source to Deploy from a branch.
external.consequence: Without it nothing is published and the file does nothing. Nothing in this repository reports whether Pages is on.

reviews.section: whether this is the file this site wants
reviews.decision: It turns the Jekyll processor off. Take it for a site that is already built HTML -- output from a generator, or anything with a path component starting with an underscore, which Jekyll otherwise refuses to serve. A site GitHub builds with Jekyll from source wants _config.yml instead.

external.step: Place the file at the root of what Pages publishes -- the repository root for a branch source, or the root of the uploaded artifact for a workflow source.
external.consequence: Elsewhere it has no effect, and the symptom is underscore-prefixed paths silently 404ing on a site that otherwise looks fine.

slots.what: The path this site is served from, trailing slash included: "/" for a user or organization site, "/<repository-name>/" for a project site. The distinction matters here more than anywhere else on the site -- a bare "/" on a project site sends someone who already took a wrong turn out of the project entirely, onto the account's own page.

reviews.section: whether the project publishes a site at all
reviews.decision: GitHub Pages is the only thing that reads this file. In a repository with Pages off it is an HTML file nobody serves, and its presence reads as a site that exists.

reviews.section: the styling and the wording
reviews.decision: It ships generic and self-contained on purpose: every stylesheet, font, or script referenced from an error page is itself a path that can fail, and a broken 404 is the one failure nobody notices until it matters. Match it to the site's design by inlining, not by linking out. Add a search box or a link to the documentation index if the site is large enough that "back to the start" is not useful.

external.step: Place the file at the root of what Pages publishes -- the repository root for a branch source, the root of the uploaded artifact for a workflow source -- and keep the name 404.html exactly.
external.consequence: Anywhere else, Pages never finds it and serves GitHub's own 404 instead, which is indistinguishable from having no custom page because that is what it is.

external.step: After the site deploys, request a path that does not exist and confirm this page is what comes back.
external.consequence: It is the one page on the site no link points at, so it is the one page that stays broken unnoticed.

slots.what: The `name` field, shown as the environment's label in Codespaces and in the editor's remote indicator. The same answer as the title asked for CITATION.cff and CONTRIBUTING.md.

reviews.section: the image, and the features added to it
reviews.decision: It ships as the generic Debian base image with no features, which builds and gives a shell and nothing else -- deliberately, because the toolchains a repository needs are exactly what the template cannot know. Add the language features this repository's manifests require, or replace the image outright. An unchanged image is not broken, it is empty, and the failure shows up as a missing compiler at the first build rather than at container creation. Every feature added here is version-pinned and nothing bumps it: add `package-ecosystem: devcontainers` to .github/dependabot.yml in the same edit. The file ships without it because an ecosystem entry naming a manifest the repository does not have fails with dependency_file_not_found rather than being skipped, so the entry is wrong until the first feature exists and required from then on.

reviews.section: the image tag
reviews.decision: bookworm is a mutable tag, and a dev container is rebuilt without being asked -- Codespaces and the editors do it on their own -- so what the tag resolves to changes under the repository with no diff. The alternative is not strictly better: nothing here bumps a digest either, since Dependabot's devcontainers ecosystem updates Features and not the base image, so a pinned digest goes stale as silently as a tag moves. Pin it where a reproducible environment matters more than picking up patches, and put a calendar reminder behind the pin rather than a bot. What makes the tag tolerable as the default is that the shipped file adds no features, no mounts, and no postCreateCommand, so a changed base image runs nothing this repository wrote.

reviews.section: the absent lifecycle command
reviews.decision: No postCreateCommand ships. scripts/doctor is the natural candidate once the image carries the toolchains it checks, and the wrong one before that: it would report every missing toolchain at creation and make a working container look broken. Add it in the same edit that adds the features it verifies.

reviews.section: the root manifest the first tool needs
reviews.decision: The warning this file carries is the whole reason it is worth copying: scripts/check runs from the repository root and reads the manifests it finds there, so a tool with its own go.mod or pyproject.toml and no root counterpart is linted, tested, and built by nobody, with nothing reporting the gap. Add the root manifest in the same change that adds the first tool.

reviews.section: the Ownership list
reviews.decision: It ships as a shape -- one `tools/<name>/` bullet standing for an entry -- because the template cannot know what this directory will hold. Replace it with the real directories as they arrive, one line each. Left as shipped, the file documents a boundary while leaving the directory itself unnavigable, which is worse than no file: a reader who finds this one stops looking.

reviews.section: registering it with the parent
reviews.decision: The documentation contract is walked from the root downward through Child Index entries, so a child CLAUDE.md no parent lists is never read. Add tools/CLAUDE.md to the root CLAUDE.md's Child Index in the same change that adopts it.
